title: Want to Support Your Child's Mental Health? Doctors Say Start With Sleep
excerpt: Growing research links poor sleep in childhood and adolescence to anxiety, behavioral issues and even psychosis risk in adulthood
body:
• Children who chronically sleep too little are more than twice as likely to develop a psychotic disorder in early adulthood, according to a major study in JAMA Psychiatry
  • Poor sleep health in adolescence is linked to higher hospitalization rates and lower life satisfaction in young adulthood
  • Only consistent, quality sleep — not weekend catch-up — protects children's cognitive function, emotional regulation and peer relationships
  • Experts recommend limiting screens before bed, maintaining consistent sleep schedules and ensuring one hour of daily physical activity

When parents look for ways to support their child's emotional wellbeing, the answer may be simpler — and more foundational — than they expect. A growing body of research shows that sleep is one of the most powerful levers for protecting children's mental health, with effects that ripple well into adulthood.

A landmark study published in JAMA Psychiatry, based on data from more than 12,000 children tracked from infancy to age 24, found that children with persistently short sleep durations were more than twice as likely to develop a psychotic disorder in early adulthood and nearly four times as likely to experience psychotic episodes.

More Than Just Tiredness

The consequences of poor sleep in children go far beyond crankiness. Research from Massachusetts General Hospital found that children who don't get enough sleep between ages three and seven experience measurable challenges in attention, emotional control and peer relationships by mid-childhood.

"It's entirely normal for children to suffer from sleep problems at different points in their childhood, but it's also important to know when it might be time to seek help. Sometimes sleep can become a persistent and chronic problem, and this is where we see links with psychiatric illness in adulthood."

— Dr. Isabel Morales-Muñoz, University of Birmingham

Separate research tracking adolescents into young adulthood found that poor sleep regularity and insomnia symptoms in the teenage years were linked to higher rates of hospitalization and lower life satisfaction by age 22. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends that teenagers aged 13 to 18 should get eight to ten hours of sleep on a regular basis for optimal health.

Why It's Getting Harder

Screen time is a major disruptor. Multiple studies have shown that electronic devices interfere with the body's production of melatonin, the hormone that regulates sleep-wake cycles. Children appear to be particularly sensitive to this effect. The blue light from phones and tablets, combined with stimulating content, can delay sleep onset and reduce sleep quality even when total time in bed seems adequate.

Overscheduled afternoons and inconsistent bedtimes compound the problem. Many families, particularly in high-achieving diaspora communities where academic and extracurricular pressures run high, inadvertently sacrifice sleep for productivity.

What Parents Can Do

Sleep experts recommend several evidence-based strategies:

Set a consistent bedtime. Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, with no more than one hour of variation on weekends. Weekend sleep catch-up does not compensate for weeknight deficits.

Create a wind-down routine. Allow quiet time before bed — reading, calm music, or gentle conversation. No screens for at least 30 to 60 minutes before lights out.

Keep the bedroom dark and cool. A sleep-friendly environment signals the brain to produce melatonin naturally.

Prioritize physical activity. At least one hour of vigorous play or exercise daily helps children fall asleep faster and sleep more deeply.

Watch for warning signs. Persistent irritability, poor focus, frequent accidents and sudden changes in school performance can all indicate inadequate sleep.

When to Seek Help

If a child consistently struggles to fall asleep, wakes frequently, snores loudly or shows signs of persistent fatigue despite adequate time in bed, it may be time to consult a pediatrician or sleep specialist. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) has been shown to be more effective than medication for treating sleep issues in children.

The research is clear: investing in a child's sleep is one of the most impactful things a parent can do for their long-term mental health. It costs nothing, requires no special equipment and the benefits compound over a lifetime.
